The platform could make those observations visible by location and service provider, while TRAI and providers interpret them alongside independent drive-test data. This is a hypothetical illustration, not a reported event.

pocketRead.excerpt: TRAI’s Network Anubhav Platform brings user and independent drive-test observations into a geospatial dashboard, with web access to DND facilities.

question.answer: It can improve transparency and help consumers, providers and TRAI act on location-specific evidence; however, user-test coverage and methodology limitations mean that dashboard observations should complement, not replace, standardised assessments.
question.prompt: How should a regulator use a geospatial telecom dashboard without treating user-generated observations as a complete quality assessment?

sections.heading: A regulatory dashboard for network experience
paragraphs: On 4 November 2026, TRAI launched the Network Anubhav Platform. It combines test results from TRAI’s MySpeed and MyCall apps with TRAI independent drive-test data and displays network observations through geospatial maps.

Users can examine cellular and fixed-broadband results by service provider and technology, including download and upload-speed parameters. The platform also provides filters, supporting tables and downloadable reports.

sections.heading: Transparency with a defined limitation
paragraphs: The platform shows percentile values from user tests, including P50, P80 for mobile broadband and P90 for fixed broadband, as described in the official release. The release cautions that user-test values do not constitute a comprehensive assessment based on standard methodology.

The dashboard can nevertheless provide useful information about other users’ experience at particular locations. Telecom providers can use location, time and technical-parameter data for network analysis, while TRAI can use aggregated insights for monitoring and network-performance improvement.

sections.heading: Consumer control beyond network maps
paragraphs: The platform provides web access to DND facilities. Consumers can set preferences for commercial communication, submit complaints about unsolicited commercial communication, track complaint status and view consolidated and service-provider-wise complaint information.

The MySpeed SDK also permits eligible third-party applications to integrate connectivity-measurement capabilities. Wider participation may expand the volume and coverage of real-world measurements, but interpretation should continue to account for representativeness and methodological limits.

advisory_notes: The source extract is dated 4 November 2026, while the supplied retrievedAt value is only a download time; the note correctly uses the document’s stated date.
“MySpeed SDK enables eligible third-party apps” is supported by the supplied release, but the proposed participation and coverage benefits are analytical implications rather than reported outcomes.
Claims about privacy, demographic representativeness, digital inclusion, and targeted investment are reasonable UPSC analysis but are not established facts in the release.
“Strengthens consumer participation in governance” is evaluative framing; the source supports consumer contribution and access, not a measured governance outcome.
The statutory mandate and detailed TRAI functions are asserted in the note but are not demonstrated by the supplied extract; retain only after separate primary-source verification.

The proposed anchors are broadly relevant: e-governance, transparency, consumer protection, statutory regulation, and technology-driven governance fit GS2; GS3.6 is weaker and should be retained only if explicitly tied to technology applica
The pocketRead statement that the platform can help providers and TRAI act on location-specific evidence is an inference, though the release supports provider analysis and TRAI monitoring uses.
The hypothetical locality example is clearly labelled as an illustration and does not present a real event; its mechanism is consistent with the platform description.

wayForward: Publish clear methodology, coverage limitations and interpretation guidance for dashboard indicators.
Use user-generated observations alongside independent drive tests and standardised quality-of-service assessments.
Expand participation through accessible interfaces and eligible third-party integrations while protecting privacy and preventing misuse of location-linked data.
Enable telecom providers and TRAI to convert recurring localised observations into transparent, time-bound network-improvement actions.
